1.s: In a famine Naomi’s family moves to Moab, where her husband and sons die. Naomi returns home, and her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her: “Your people will be my people, and your God my God.”
1.d: The events took place around 1100 BC, in the time of the judges [[tosn:Ruth 1:1]]. Ruth “clung” to Naomi, the same Hebrew word used for husband and wife being joined [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]], and made her promise in the LORD’s name [[tosn:Ruth 1:16-17]]. Naomi asks to be called Mara, “bitter” [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].

2.s: Ruth gleans barley in the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi’s husband, who treats her with great kindness.
2.d: Gleaning was one of God’s laws to feed the poor [[tosn:Ruth 2:2]] [[bible:Leviticus 19:9-10]]. As Elimelech’s relative, Boaz could act as family redeemer [[tosn:Ruth 2:1]]. He blesses Ruth by the God “under whose wings you have come to take refuge”, a picture of a bird protecting its young [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]] [[bible:Ruth 2:12]].

3.s: At Naomi’s suggestion Ruth goes to Boaz at night on the threshing floor and asks him to spread his garment over her: to marry and redeem her.
3.d: “Spread the corner of your garment over your servant” was Ruth’s way of asking Boaz to marry her [[tosn:Ruth 3:9]] [[bible:Ezekiel 16:8]]. Boaz protects her reputation by sending her home before daylight [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].

4.s: Boaz redeems the family land and marries Ruth. Their son Obed is the grandfather of King David.
4.d: Boaz joins the duty of a family redeemer with the duty of marrying a dead relative’s widow [[tosn:Ruth 4:5]]. The women say Ruth is “better to you than seven sons”, more than the greatest family blessing of the time [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]]. The closing family line leads to David [[tosn:Ruth 4:18-22]], and Ruth appears in Jesus’s family tree [[bible:Matthew 1:5]].
